headline: High: xonsh can write and execute shell commands against filesystem state while plano can ingest and emit API-backed outputs, creating default-path data leakage and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, but xonsh can read stdin/stdout and filesystem contents while plano can call an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint and handle config files. If plano outputs are copied into xonsh or files are shared, prompt-like content could be reinterpreted. The pairwise pathway is plausible but not default.
conditions: IF plano outputs are manually copied into xonsh stdin/stdout or shared files
IF xonsh treats file or terminal content as executable shell input
mitigations: Keep plano and xonsh on separate workspaces
Disable copy-paste of model outputs into shell prompts
Use a strict prompt/template wrapper for any handoff
Review any file-based handoff before execution

B_data_leakage.rationale: xonsh reads and writes the filesystem and broad network egress is enabled, while plano also has broad network egress and touches logs, traces, and metrics. A shared workspace or copied files could expose sensitive operational data from plano to xonsh outputs or external APIs. This is not proven by a shared path, but the default capabilities make leakage plausible.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same filesystem tree
IF plano logs, traces, or metrics contain sensitive data
IF xonsh forwards file contents or environment variables to external commands or APIs
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Redact logs and traces before any shell processing
Restrict xonsh access to sensitive files
Audit outbound commands for file-content exfiltration
Use a throwaway workspace for shared artifacts

C_capability_conflict.rationale: plano does not request filesystem write or shell execution, while xonsh can write the filesystem and execute shell commands. There is overlap only on broad network egress and file access, but no documented shared mutable resource or locking conflict. The interaction is therefore limited unless an operator deliberately couples them.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same writable directory
IF an operator uses xonsh to mutate files that plano also reads
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Avoid concurrent edits to shared files
Use file locks for any shared artifact
Keep git operations outside the pair

D_cascading_error.rationale: plano can produce API-backed routing or configuration outputs, and xonsh can execute shell commands and spawn subprocesses. If xonsh consumes plano output as authoritative instructions, a mistaken or malicious plano result can cascade into real actions. The profiles do not show verification gates, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF xonsh executes commands derived from plano output without human review
IF plano output is used as a source of truth for shell automation
mitigations: Require manual review before execution
Add a validation step between plano and xonsh
Log and diff proposed commands before running them
Use allowlisted command templates

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and touch operational data rather than explicit regulated classes. Plano handles logs, traces, and metrics; xonsh handles filesystem contents, source code, configuration, and environment variables. A compliance issue would arise only if regulated data is placed into those surfaces, so this is a low, conditional risk. The other agent is cited because the concern is pairwise data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is stored in the shared workspace
IF retention or residency requirements differ between the two processing paths
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared files
Apply a retention policy to logs and notebooks
Separate residency-sensitive workloads
Review data classification before handoff
